description:
We’re a Canada-based team building NASTRA, an intelligent astronaut health copilot, for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It combines physiological data, psychological well-being, and mission context to help astronauts understand their health, spot patterns, and make informed decisions in space.

From Canadian maple roots to Martian soil.
summary:
NASTRA is an astronaut health copilot for long-duration missions, including future missions to Mars, where real-time medical support from Earth may not always be available.

We designed NASTRA to stand by for the moment when health data changes unexpectedly or a crew member reports that something feels wrong. It combines vitals, sleep, self-reported mood, mission schedule, previous health events and relevant NASA evidence into one unified context.

NASTRA has two interfaces on one intelligence core. NASTRA Station is a one-screen crew application with a health dashboard and chat, voice and photo input. NASTRA EVA is a lightweight, voice-first helmet HUD that surfaces only abnormal or mission-relevant information.

Safety-critical decisions are never left to the AI model. Deterministic code screens for red flags before any model runs, selects the relevant protocol and controls escalation. Gemma 4 interprets crew input and communicates from code-selected context, while validation blocks unsupported diagnosis and false reassurance.

NASTRA compares measurements against each crew member’s own baseline and can generate a structured evidence handover for a flight surgeon.

The prototype achieved 28/28 safety evaluations, 108 automated tests and 0 detected WCAG 2.2 AA violations. All crew health data are simulated.
details:
What NASTRA does and how it works

NASTRA is an astronaut health copilot designed to support crew health autonomy during long-duration missions, particularly future missions where communication with Earth may be delayed or temporarily unavailable.

Our starting point was simple: astronauts may already have physiological telemetry, sleep data, activity records, psychological self-reports, mission schedules and medical knowledge, but these signals do not automatically become useful context when a crew member suddenly says that something feels wrong.

NASTRA turns that moment into a structured health event.

When a crew member reports a symptom or concern, a deterministic safety screen runs before any AI model is called. It looks for predefined red-flag language and can immediately raise the urgency of the event. The model then interprets the crew member’s message into structured information, such as the type of request, health domain and relevant context. Code routes the event into one of four prototype health workflows and controls what happens next.

The protocol engine determines which follow-up questions are required, which tools may be used and whether escalation is necessary. Quick replies are resolved by code rather than generated freely by the model, and urgency within an event can only increase.

Allow-listed tools retrieve only the information relevant to the active event. Depending on the situation, this can include current vitals, sleep, self-reported mood or stress, mission schedule, recent activity, previous health events and relevant NASA Human Research Program knowledge.

The language model receives this curated context and generates a concise explanation. Its output is then validated by code. Unsupported diagnosis, false reassurance, unsupported causal claims and ungrounded numerical statements are rejected. If validation fails, the system can retry and ultimately fall back to deterministic facts rather than presenting an unsafe model response.

If escalation is required, NASTRA builds a structured handover in code rather than relying on the model. The handover includes the trigger in the crew member’s own words, relevant warning signs, flagged measurements, conversation history and the current protocol state. In the prototype, this is sent to a simulated ground console representing flight-surgeon handover.

Two forms, one intelligence and safety core

NASTRA has two interfaces designed for different operational environments.

NASTRA Station is the primary crew-computer application. It provides a single-screen health workspace with natural-language conversation, voice input, photo input, current health context, personal baseline comparisons, alerts, historical events and protocol state. The interface is designed so that important information remains visible without requiring the crew member to search through multiple pages during a stressful moment.

NASTRA EVA is a lightweight helmet-HUD concept for situations where hands and attention are occupied. Instead of reproducing the full Station dashboard, it follows an exception-based approach and surfaces only flagged or mission-relevant information. The current EVA prototype includes a voice-driven demonstration for comparing present telemetry with the same time on the previous day.

Both interfaces share the same underlying safety logic, health-event structure, protocols and data.

Personal and longitudinal context

A central design goal was to avoid treating a measurement as meaningful simply because it is above or below a generic number.

NASTRA compares relevant measurements with the individual crew member’s own recent history. For example, post-exercise heart rate can be compared with that same person’s typical values at the same number of minutes after exercise.

Our prototype baseline monitor can create an Advisory when a measurement deviates substantially from the person’s own 14-day baseline or when repeated short sleep periods are detected. These are prototype contextual rules, not clinical thresholds. A Warning can only come from the deterministic safety and escalation pathway.

NASTRA also searches structured history for similar previous events and their outcomes. Historical similarity can add useful context, but it never overrides the current safety screen. A previous benign episode cannot make a new event safe, and an association is never presented as proof of causation.

NASA and CSA resources

The prototype directly ingests six NASA Human Research Program risk resources into its knowledge system. The documents are chunked, embedded locally and retrieved according to the active health context. The knowledge search was tested across seven representative queries, with 7/7 retrieving the intended NASA risk resource.

We also used NASA’s Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, ongoing Human Research Program research, NASA-STD-3001 and related longitudinal-health guidance as design and domain references. CSA Bio-Monitor resources informed the physiological channels represented in our simulated crew data.

We deliberately distinguish authoritative reference material from crew data. All astronaut physiological, psychological and mission records in the current prototype are simulated.

Technology

The application is built with Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript and Zod.

The current language and vision model is Gemma 4 26B A4B, accessed through OpenRouter behind an OpenAI-compatible provider interface. This keeps the inference layer replaceable without changing the rest of the NASTRA architecture.

Speech-to-text runs locally through Whisper tiny.en using Transformers.js. The transcript is placed into the conversation composer for crew review and is never automatically submitted.

NASA knowledge embeddings are also generated locally using gte-small through Transformers.js.

The primary data layer uses Supabase with PostgreSQL and pgvector. Row Level Security is enabled and application access is server-side. Structured SQL read models are used for functions such as personal baseline comparison, post-exercise comparison, time-series retrieval and the simulated telemetry feed. PGlite with pgvector allows the same database logic and migrations to run locally for offline development and testing.

NASTRA’s interface is built on NHIS, our own NASTRA Human Interface System, using React Aria components for accessible interaction primitives. The product adds a restrained aerospace/HUD visual layer without changing the underlying accessibility model.

The EVA prototype uses standard web technologies rather than a 3D engine: Canvas 2D, HTML5 video, SVG displacement mapping and CSS clip-path are used to project the HUD onto the visor footage.

Privacy and multimodal input

NASTRA supports photo input, but the model is restricted to describing visible information. Code removes observations that attempt to name a medical condition, infer a cause or infer an emotional state. The crew member reviews and confirms the extracted observations before they are used. Photos are processed in memory and are not stored server-side.

The same principle applies to voice input: speech is transcribed locally and remains editable before submission.

Testing and failure-driven development

We treated failures as part of the product design rather than testing only successful demonstrations.

One of our most important tests simulated a crew member deteriorating from breathing difficulty to being barely able to stand and then typing only “hel”. The first version of NASTRA repeatedly asked the same safety question and failed to escalate correctly.

We identified and fixed multiple causes, including insufficient red-flag phrasing, missing near-collapse handling, repeated unanswered safety questions, urgency decreasing across turns and an escalation path that claimed to notify ground without actually creating an alert.

That full interaction is now preserved as a permanent regression test.

The current prototype has achieved 28/28 on the message-understanding evaluation, 28/28 on the deterministic safety evaluation, 7/7 on the NASA knowledge retrieval test and 108 automated tests overall.

We also audited all six product pages using axe-core against WCAG 2.2 AA and currently detect zero violations in the tested states, including active protocol and escalation states.

Creativity and intended impact

NASTRA’s main innovation is not simply adding a language model to a health dashboard.

The model is deliberately constrained. Code controls safety, protocol routing, tools, escalation, personal-baseline calculations and output validation. The model primarily interprets human language and communicates from context selected by the system.

This allows NASTRA to connect four dimensions around one event: what the astronaut feels, what their body is doing, what they are doing in the mission and what has happened to them before.

The intended impact is greater crew autonomy as missions move farther from Earth. NASTRA is designed to help a crew member understand their available health context immediately while producing a structured, evidence-rich handover when professional medical support is required.

Limitations

NASTRA is a concept prototype, not an operational medical system.

All current crew data are simulated. The red-flag rules and protocol content would require review and validation by qualified aerospace medical professionals before operational use. The current Gemma inference runs through a hosted endpoint rather than fully onboard. The EVA voice sequence is scripted for the demonstration, and the visor footage used in the prototype is AI-generated.

NASTRA is not affiliated with, endorsed by or approved by NASA or CSA, is not a medical device, and is not intended to replace a flight surgeon.
